summary_md: Mairesse, Walker, Mehl and Moore (JAIR 30, 2007) is the source of the SMOreg personality models that Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh ran on congressional floor speech. Those RKH estimates are the targets the lexical Big Five weights are now fitted to. The paper trains classifiers, regressors and RankBoost rankers on LIWC, MRC, speech-act and prosody features. It uses two corpora: 2,479 student essays with self-reports, and 96 EAR speakers with self-reports plus averaged ratings from 18 observers. Three results bear on the system. (1) On essays the signal is weak. In regression, only openness (r 0.33) and emotional stability (r 0.24) beat the mean baseline, and SMOreg is significant only for openness (Table 17). The system's 07-03 essays refit landed in the same weak band and was later replaced by the RKH refit. (2) Ramey footnote 4 says RKH used the observer-trained models, which are the EAR models with n = 96. In Table 19, SMOreg on EAR observer ratings is worse than predicting the mean for every trait, with relative errors from 131.75 to 213.20 percent. The reference instrument behind the held-out r of .350 against RKH therefore had no demonstrated out-of-sample accuracy in its own paper. (3) Observer-rated personality is easier to model than self-report in conversation, and emotional stability has the lowest inter-observer agreement (pair r .29). This fits the system's choice of observer gold panels and its weak N results. Prosody helps extraversion most. In self-reports, neuroticism goes with low, constant voice intensity, which supports the 2026-07-09 finding that the audio ES composite was mis-signed. No result here was reproduced by a second path, so the bearings are UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: SMOreg trained on EAR observer ratings (n = 96 speakers, 10-fold CV) has relative absolute error above the mean baseline for all five traits: E 140.05, ES 162.05, A 173.97, C 131.75, O 213.20 percent (baseline 100). The authors say SVMs and linear regression need more data than EAR provides. Ramey et al. footnote 4 states RKH used the models trained on independent observer data.
bearings.paper_location: Table 19 and Sec 5.2, p.481-482; Ramey et al. 2016 p.2 fn 4
bearings.system_side: fit_smoreg_rkh.py fits per-trait weights to RKH per-member trait averages as targets. The active mairesse_smoreg.json holds the RKH refit for all five traits as of v6, and the brain records held-out r vs RKH (E .510, mean .350) as convergence with congressional ground truth.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds if RKH used the Personality Recognizer SMOreg observer model as their fn 4 and p.2 text say. The distributed model is fit on all 96 speakers, so CV error estimates its accuracy on new speakers, and floor speech is a further genre shift. Ramey fn 8 reports SMOreg vs M5 made little difference in their data. Convergence with RKH measures agreement with a model of undemonstrated accuracy, not trait validity.

bearings.paper_claim: On the essays corpus, the trait signal is weak. In binary classification SMO reaches 55 to 62 percent (openness 62.1 vs 50.3 baseline). In regression, SMOreg relative error is E 100.65, ES 98.35, A 100.28, C 99.30 (none significant) and O 94.19 (significant). Best Pearson r is 0.33 for openness and 0.24 for emotional stability. E, A and C regressions do not beat the mean.
bearings.paper_location: Table 12 p.475; Table 17 and Sec 5.2 p.480
bearings.system_side: fit_smoreg_essays.py refit a LinearSVR on essays.csv binary y/n labels (a regression on 0/1 targets, not the continuous scores Mairesse regressed on) and reported binary CV of 53-58 percent. Weights from this fit were active 07-03 and were then replaced trait by trait with the RKH refit.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Same feature family (LIWC-analog plus Empath, not licensed LIWC or MRC). The paper's weak essay-to-trait signal for E, A and C explains why the essays fit carried little usable signal and supports abandoning it. The grid search also reports its maximum CV accuracy over 12 settings on the same folds, which is optimistic.

bearings.paper_claim: On EAR, observer-rated models beat baseline (Naive Bayes E 73.0 vs 47.8, ES 73.9 vs 51.1, C 67.7) while no self-report classifier or regressor beats baseline. Mean inter-observer pair r is .54 for E, .51 for C and only .29 for ES.
bearings.system_side: Trait validity is judged against Senate insider and academic expert panels (observer ratings), evaluated separately. E and A pass both panels; N passes insiders only.
bearings.transfer_conditions: EAR observers rated strangers from audio snippets, while Senate panels rate known public figures, so reputation enters panel ratings. Low observer agreement on ES predicts that N/ES will be the noisiest gold criterion, which matches the system's insiders-only N pass.

bearings.paper_claim: Prosody is the strongest single feature set for extraversion: RankBoost ranking loss 0.26 with prosody only (random 0.50), and Naive Bayes 67.6 percent with prosody alone. Self-assessed neurotics have low and constant voice intensity (low Int-mean and Int-stddev), a marker observers do not use.
bearings.paper_location: Table 22 p.485; Table 15 p.477; Sec 3.3 p.469-470 (Tables 10-11)
bearings.system_side: The audio pilot put its incremental-validity bar on E (BAR 1). Its BAR-2 ES_acoustic composite treated low loudness variation as ES-positive, and the 2026-07-09 note marks this composite as mis-signed.
bearings.transfer_conditions: EAR observers rated from the same audio, so prosody-to-observer gains are partly shared-channel. EAR is n = 96 lapel-mic everyday speech, while the system uses broadcast and floor clips with venue confounds. The paper supports the corrected sign direction only for self-reported neuroticism.

bearings.paper_claim: Emotional stability is expressed differently across datasets. Only a high word count and a low mean pitch mark ES in both self and observer reports in conversation. Self-references and negative-emotion words mark neuroticism in essays, but observed ES in conversation instead tracks swearing and anger words.
bearings.system_side: The genre transfer of interview N to floor and hearing text failed (rho .050, .161). emit_affective_n.py now keeps the LIWC i + negemo - posemo score only as a convergent anchor (r +.24), no longer as a component.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Paper compares essays and student conversation, not political genres. Its instability of ES markers across sources is consistent with the system's failed N genre transfer and its demotion of the LIWC term.

gaps_exposed: The docstrings at big5_traits.py:13-16 and fit_smoreg_essays.py:4-5 describe the RKH/Mairesse model as essays-trained SMOreg, but Ramey fn 4 says RKH used the observer-trained (EAR) models. The essays refit replicated the wrong arm, and the docstring still describes published-correlate linear weights that the active JSON overrides.
No external check of RKH itself: the held-out r vs RKH (mean .350) is reported as accuracy, but the source model's own CV error on EAR observer ratings was above the mean baseline for every trait.
fit_smoreg_essays.py regresses on binary y/n labels and reports the best of 12 grid settings on the same folds, with no nested CV.
The component card for affective-n still lists the LIWC term as a component; the code at emit_affective_n.py:41-43 says it is now an anchor only.
Ranking loss (pairwise order) is never used as an evaluation metric, although the paper finds ranking models best overall and the system's consumers use ranks.
flags: Brain wording conflict: the v6 note calls held-out r vs RKH congressional ground truth and calls E .51 acquaintance-level accuracy. Per this paper (Table 19) and Ramey fn 4, RKH is the output of a model with no demonstrated out-of-sample accuracy, so the figure is method agreement on n = 146, not accuracy. It needs an UNVALIDATED or method-shared label.
Provenance error: system docstrings say Ramey used Mairesse's essays SMOreg; Ramey fn 4 says observer-trained models. This is an actual factual error in the code documentation.

Ramey p.2 says SMOreg best recovers personality in written trials, but this paper's Table 17 shows SMOreg significant only for openness on essays and Table 19 shows it worse than baseline on EAR. The citation chain overstates the source.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotated entry for this paper. His position on the lexical component (Ramey is dated but foundational, and each venue needs its own framework) is reinforced. The model RKH inherits was trained on 96 student conversations and never shown to generalise beyond them, and the paper itself warns that no cross-corpus test was run. His notes do not mention that the RKH targets now drive all five active weights. The system's move from essays weights to an RKH refit replaced weak but real signal with agreement with an unvalidated instrument. That point is newer than his notes.

related.why: RKH apply this paper's pre-trained SMOreg (observer-trained, fn 4) to 1996-2014 floor speech; their per-member estimates are the system's fitting targets.
Pennebaker's LIWC program and the essays corpus (Pennebaker and King 1999) supply this paper's features and self-report data; the trait correlates in Sec 2 come from that line.
Meta-analysis of LIWC to Big Five correlations gives the population-level effect sizes that bound what Mairesse-style closed-vocabulary models can recover.
Expert observer ratings of senators are the kind of observer criterion this paper finds easier to model than self-report.
Takes up the self-reported personality recognition problem that Mairesse found intractable on conversational data, using personalised models.
Review of personality computing that positions Mairesse 2007 as a foundational benchmark and discusses its validity threats.
